author: Mohammed Altaj
title: Israel Above the Law … Palestine Beyond Justice
content:
The world did not lack knowledge of what was happening to Palestinians.

It knew that a people had been living under occupation for decades; that land was being confiscated, settlements expanding, homes demolished, and checkpoints cutting cities and villages off from one another.

The United Nations knew. Governments knew. Parliaments and international courts knew.

The shift now visible across significant parts of Western public opinion did not begin because the world suddenly discovered new facts about Palestine.

What changed was the distance between the news and the human being.

People saw what war means when a child is trapped beneath rubble, what displacement means when a family carries whatever it can and walks away without knowing where it will go.

And the numbers began to acquire names, faces and voices.

One of those names was Hind Rajab.

I do not mention Hind because her story encompasses everything that happened in Gaza. I mention her because some tragedies become windows through which people see what numbers alone cannot reveal.

Hind was trapped inside a car in Gaza in January 2024 after members of her family had been killed. She called for help. Twelve days later, she was found dead inside the car. The two paramedics sent to rescue her were also found dead.

But Hind was no longer a number.

author: Paul Buhle
title: The Communitarian Mind of Michael Albert
content:
Somewhere, in the complex and often confused history of anarchist and communitarian movements of the US, Michael Albert resides, now almost 80, a veteran of endless campaigns but still eager to make his familiar points. Communitarianism of some kind can work, can create a substitute for the miserable economic arrangements of the present, and engage ordinary people in the process of changing themselves as they endeavor to change the world.

This sentiment has a more than honorable history even in the US, historically known for its weak and fragile Left institutions. Its origins should properly be placed well before the rise of the Marxist-related movements, mostly German immigrants, during the 1860s-70s. Indeed, the communitarian experiments of the 1820s-40s engaged some of the great figures of the age, from Shakers to Bohemians, and even produced a remarkable literature, including Nathaniel Hawthorne’s rather satirical Blithedale Romance.

The ideas of dress reform (mainly for women), healthy foods, and even freer sexual relations flowed into Abolitionist and Women’s Rights movements. The Civil War swallowed a large chunk of utopianism, but enough survived to prompt a rebirth in successive generations. author: Mahdi Niksefat Motlagh
title: Ending the war requires accepting Iran in the Middle East
content:
The hardest question about ending the war with Iran belongs in Washington. What place can Iran occupy after the fighting stops? A country left economically excluded, unable to rebuild and exposed to renewed attack has little reason to regard a ceasefire as a durable ending. The war cannot be politically settled while Iranian recovery remains an unacceptable outcome.

The latest diplomacy leaves that question unresolved. Tehran has received US feedback, through Qatar, on a seven-day trust-building proposal. Yet on 1 October, the US Treasury expanded sanctions against Iran’s automotive and rail sectors, alongside manufacturing and steel networks. Talks about ending the confrontation are proceeding alongside measures that further restrict Iran’s capacity to sustain its economy.

The Islamic Republic connects these claims to a revolutionary and religious account of its purpose. Ali Khamenei’s 2019 Second Phase statement, with its emphasis on building an Islamic civilisation, expressed that connection explicitly. Security, within this understanding, includes the capacity to continue a political project.

author: Abe Walker
title: The Battle for the Soul of the UAW: Union Democracy and the Seductions of Power
content:
After years of struggling in relative obscurity, democratic socialists were jubilant to have elected one of their own to high-profile office. With bold rhetoric and meme-friendly soundbites, their candidate captured the hearts and minds of a working-class base eager for an alternative to the establishment’s caustic brand of demagoguery. Ignoring calls for moderation, the campaign took on a defiant, openly confrontational tone. Its outcome shocked the old guard, upended the status quo, and served as a warning to entrenched interests everywhere.

The year was 2023, and Shawn Fain had just won the presidency of the United Auto Workers union. Fain quickly became the public face of a resurgent workers movement that seemed poised to usher in a new wave of labor militancy. But there would be little time for celebration once the weight of the task ahead set in. Indeed – like a certain big city mayor – Fain would quickly discover that his election fight was only a preview of the battles to come.

Fain is now standing for reelection, with ballots set to be tallied next month. Three years ago, few could imagine that Fain would face a viable challenger as he eyed a second term. Yet today, his star has long since dimmed, and his fate now hangs in balance. author: Patrick Egan
title: White Nationalism’s Appeal Runs Deeper Than Partisan Politics
content:
As Americans prepared to celebrate the nation’s 250th birthday on the morning of July 4, sobering images flashed across their phones and TV screens. Hundreds of masked men marched the streets of Washington carrying flags and chanting “Reclaim America!” It soon became clear from the logos on their identical baseball caps that the marchers were members of Patriot Front, a white nationalist group.

The march ended without incident. Still, it joined the 2017 “Unite the Right” rally in Charlottesville, Virginia, and the Jan. 6, 2021, attack on the U.S. Capitol – both of which culminated in deadly violence – as recent mass demonstrations with participants who openly embrace white nationalism. Members of a loosely organized movement that usually operates out of public view, white nationalists hold that shifting demographics pose an existential threat to the white race, which they view as culturally superior and deserving of power over other groups in the U.S.

Combined with the spread of white nationalist ideology from obscure corners of the internet into mainstream politics, these events have led many Americans to wonder: How extensive is white nationalism’s appeal among the broader public, and who is drawn to this extremist ideology?

author: Branko Marcetic
title: According to Polls, Americans Like Socialism a Lot
content:
A crop of recent polls shows that socialism’s appeal is surprisingly broad. They also reflect a transformed US political landscape that is ripe for a socialist politician to capitalize on — if they’re willing to step up.

Socialism is more popular than it’s been for a long time, both socialism and its most well-known adherents appeal to a surprisingly diverse voter base, and most people still have no idea who Hasan Piker is.

Those are just a few of the takeaways from a crop of polls conducted over the past month or so, which together suggest the radicalized, antiestablishment zeal that’s taken over the Democratic electorate and opened the door for a rising socialist insurgency is still going strong, with a few surprises in tow. And they come at a potentially crucial time, as socialist Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez weighs whether to make a run for president in 2028, a campaign that many socialists view as pivotal to the future prospects of their movement as a whole.

We should obviously be careful with polls, which are not actual elections and only give us an imperfect snapshot of public opinion at any point in time. Still, while they may not exactly reflect hard numbers, they do often reflect real trends, especially when put alongside other poll results. And as such, these recent ones offer several takeaways.

author: D K Renton
title: Forgiveness is Part of Socialism
content:
When I tell people I’m interested in the politics of forgiveness, that often surprises them: the idea sounds bad and moralistic. I invite them to consider that the whole point of a revolution is to start over. The people who will change the world must start in this one — a system that rewards selfishness and cruelty. Accepting people despite their past harms is a fundamental part of building a new society.

Some socialists say that the left doesn’t need ethics. Marx and Engels wrote that Communism would end morality: ‘Communism abolishes eternal truths, it abolishes all religion, and all morality.’ But Marx also said that if Communism won, life would follow different rules: ‘From each according to his ability, to each according to his needs.’ What’s that, if not a description of a better society? In The German Ideology, Marx says this about revolutions: in them, we rid ourselves of ‘all the muck of ages and become fitted to found society anew.’ People change; without that possibility, you couldn’t have socialism.

When writing about forgiveness, there are three big ideas that matter most to me. First, forgiveness is an act done by victims — not their friends, and definitely not the state. The victim must achieve justice. Afterwards, you ask them if they want to forgive: in a situation of ongoing harm, asking a victim isn’t an act of generosity; it’s cruel.

Last week, the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD) counted what remained of Gaza’s economy after almost three years of genocide and almost two decades of siege. Ninety-two per cent of its economic establishments have been damaged or destroyed. Unemployment has reached 78 per cent. GDP per person fell to $212 last year — barely 17 per cent of its pre-genocide level — while less than 1.5 per cent of Gaza’s cropland remains accessible and undamaged. Recovery and reconstruction will cost at least $71.5 billion. Pedro Manuel Moreno, acting head of UNCTAD, called it “the world’s most severe economic crisis on record”.

author: Céli Pinto
title: The Most Important Election in Brazilian History
content:
We usually say that in general elections, we’re choosing a president, governors and lawmakers for the next four years. That much seems obvious. But in this election, with the first round on October 4 and the runoff on October 25, we’re not just choosing who governs. We’re choosing the country’s future for decades to come.

This isn’t a choice between candidate A and candidate B. It’s a choice between a sharp lurch toward colonized totalitarianism and the survival of democracy. Every voter needs to have this clearly in mind. We are responsible for this country’s future. Future generations will blame us, and rightly so, if we fail and Brazil is handed over to colonizer vultures.

Voters, whether or not they are politically active, whether they are young, middle-aged or elderly, have plenty of issues with the current government. It’s true the government could have done more, particularly if it didn’t have a Congress dedicated almost exclusively to serving its own interests. Even so, the government accomplished a great deal. It did this not despite Congress, but because Congress exists. That made it possible to negotiate with lawmakers and to pressure them through the press and social media.

author: Binoy Kampmark
title: Denial as a Way of Life: Netanyahu on Egyptian Warnings About October 7
content:
Things are looking bleaker by the day for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, most notably for his standing as a competent leader in full mastery of his office. After allegations were made that he had received warnings from the United Arab Emirates leader President Mohamed bin Zayed (MBZ) that the October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas was, if not imminent then certainly most likely, a sense of paralytic denial has taken hold.

The claim by Haaretz, based on research for the book Hostages: 843 Days of Abandonment by Shlomi Eldar and Ruth Yuval, finds Netanyahu being told, in unambiguous terms, that an attack by Hamas was being planned. A 45-minute conversation apparently took place between the UAE President and Netanyahu, in which the Emirati leader warned of the potentially destabilising intentions of the late Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar. Talks between Hamas and Netanyahu’s office that had begun in 2023 in search of temporary truce had stalled. Sinwar was getting testy.

The Egyptian intelligence chief Abbas Kamel has also emerged as another prominent figure to bulk the warnings on Hamas’s ominous intentions, with The Wall Street Journal reporting as much on September 27. author: Thomas Klikauer
title: German Natural Gas Politics – Profits or Ingenuity
content:
According to the IEA‘s global electricity mix, non-renewable, unsustainable and highly polluting fossil fuels still make up 57% of electricity production with the much talked about oil – Strait of Hormuz, etc. – being just 2%. Oil is used to make petrol for cars still running on combustion engines, but it is not much used to make electricity.

By contrast, renewables come in at an ever-increasing percentage with wind and solar are 17% and hydropower 14%. Not to be forgotten: the atomic power of Chernobyl and Fukushima, at 9%.

In Germany, solar makes up 33%, coal 27%, natural gas 13%, wind 11%, biomass 9% and others 7%. According to Germany’s “windmesse.de”, Germany runs on 62% renewable energy for electricity generation. Sadly, natural gas still made up 13.4%.

Worldwide, the share of natural gas in global electricity generation fell from 23.9% in 2020 to 21.8% in 2025. Still, gas remains the world’s second-largest source of electricity generation with a 22% share of total output, behind only coal at 33%. Gas makes up a much bigger slice in places like the US (40%) than in, for example, India (2%) or China (3%).

Despite all this, Germany is at a critical point in its energy transition towards renewables. While Germany’s conservative government fancies building new gas-fired power plants, this raises a fundamental question: is Germany building a bridge to a carbon-neutral age?

title: When Law Fails: A Jew Reads Confronting Zionism
content:
I am, maybe, a reader at cross-purposes from this book’s intent. I translate the challenge of fighting Zionist oppression of Palestine gentiles, somewhat automatically, also to the question, How do we redeem Jewish identity?

Confronting Zionism, by international law scholars Noura Erakat and John Reynolds, reviews the colonial and imperialist legal assumptions in the Balfour declaration, the League of Nations Mandate, and the May 1948 declaration of the State of Israel.

Once seen, it is hard to unsee, the principles that Erakat and Reynolds name as the face of Zionism to Palestinians: domination and dehumanization.

Their work is about failed attempts to use international institutions to protect Gaza since October 7, 2023, and during Zionism’s stages for the past 100 years in its accomplishment of Jewish nationalist rule of Palestine. They analyze the colonial assumptions in international structures that made the conquest feasible.
